blocks.text: 2. The Easiness and Difficulty of the Seasoned Practitioner’s Effort

inline.s: What, then, is the difficulty of the seasoned practitioner’s effort? When his effort carries him to the point where true doubt stands before him—to have awareness and illumination still belongs to birth-and-death; to have neither awareness nor illumination falls again into vacant nothingness. This ground is truly hard, and many who reach it cannot shake themselves free; they stand atop the hundred-foot pole with no way to advance.

[True doubt]The genuine doubt-sensation—probing, thought after thought without interruption, toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted. [Standing atop the hundred-foot pole, unable to advance]Daoyuan
the Chan Master’s verse reads
“A man unmoving atop the hundred-foot pole
not a single thought arising
, though he has entered, is not yet true
not ultimate
; from the hundred-foot pole he must step forward
seeing the nature through and through
, and the ten directions of the world are the whole body.”
(Jingde Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)
There are some
(certain people)

who, having reached this ground, find their effort a little under control and meet no situation they cannot break through, and so imagine that ignorance is utterly cut off and their effort has arrived home. Little do they know that they are living every day inside the cave of ignorance without knowing it. Suddenly meeting a single situation, they cannot break through it, cannot be their own master, and are carried off by it as before—how regrettable!

Or there are those who reach the ground where true doubt stands before them, and in that emptiness a little wisdom arises; having savoured a few koans of the ancients, they let go of the doubt-sensation, fancy themselves greatly awakened, chant poems and compose verses, blink their eyes and lift their brows, and call themselves good and wise teachers. Such people ruin themselves and ruin others; their offence is boundless.

There are also those who mistake the meaning of Old Man Bodhidharma’s “Outwardly, cease all conditions; inwardly, let the mind be without gasping; with a mind like a wall, one may enter the Way,” and of the Sixth Patriarch’s “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at precisely this
nèn

moment—what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?”—and so they take sitting beside a withered tree on a rocky ledge as the ultimate standard. Such people take the conjured city for the treasure city and a guest land for their native home; the old woman burning down the hut is precisely a curse upon these dead fellows.

[Misunderstanding the meaning]1. In Patriarch Bodhidharma’s instruction, “Outwardly, cease all conditions; inwardly, let the mind be without gasping; with a mind like a wall, one may enter the Way,” the phrase “one may enter the Way” means: one may begin to realize the Way. That is to say, once the first three phrases are accomplished, the preparatory work for realizing the Way is complete. Some people, however, mistakenly suppose that having accomplished “outwardly, cease all conditions; inwardly, let the mind be without gasping; with a mind like a wall” is itself the realization of the Way, is the ultimate. 2. In the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction, “Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at precisely this moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” the word “that” (nà) means “which” in modern Chinese (in the ancient language there was no character for “which”; the character for “that” carried two senses, one matching modern “that” and one matching modern “which”), and not “that” in the modern sense. Some people, however, mistakenly read “what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?” as meaning, in modern Chinese: that (That) is your original face. Hence they wrongly take “not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at precisely this moment” to be the original face.

[The conjured city]A phantom city. This is the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The place where all sentient beings attain Buddhahood is the treasure city, yet the road to that treasure city is perilous and far. The Buddha, fearing that travellers would grow weary and turn back, conjured a city midway so that they might rest a while, gather their strength, and then press straight on to the treasure city. The Buddha wished to bring all sentient beings to the fruit of Buddhahood, but because beings are timid and weak and cannot bear it, he first taught the nirvāṇa of the Lesser Vehicle, so that having attained that nirvāṇa and rested a while, they might arouse the greater resolve and advance toward the true treasure city of Great Vehicle nirvāṇa (the fruit of Buddhahood).

[The old woman burns the hut]A Chan koan: long ago an old woman supported a hermit in a hut for twenty years, and always had a young girl bring him his meals and wait on him. One day the old woman told the girl to embrace him and ask, ‘How do you feel right now?’ The hermit said, ‘A withered tree leaning on a cold rock; through three winters, no warmth.’ The girl reported this to the old woman, who said, ‘For twenty years I have supported nothing but a worldly fellow (a worldling who has not awakened).’ So she drove him away and burned down the thatched hut. The point of this koan is that the hermit took the conjured city for the treasure city (supposing the state of no-thought to be the ultimate)—able to die, but unable to live. (See the Wudeng Huiyuan, Five Lamps Meeting at the Source.)
What, then, is the easiness of the seasoned practitioner’s effort? At this point, one need only not grow complacent, not break off, and go on finely and densely
(finely and densely probing toward the moment before a single thought has sprouted)
, and in that fineness, finer still; in that subtlety, subtler still—when the time arrives, the bottom of the bucket falls out of itself
(illumining the mind and seeing the nature)
. If it does not, then find a good and wise teacher to draw out the nails and pull out the wedges.
[Drawing out the nails and pulling out the wedges]Loosening what sticks and releasing what binds.

Master Hanshan praised it in verse: “High atop the mountain peak, / on every side no bound is seen; / I sit in stillness, unknown to all, / a lonely moon on the cold spring. / Within the spring there is no moon; / the moon is there in the blue sky. / I sing this little song of mine: / within the song no Chan you’ll find.”
The first two lines
(“High atop the mountain peak, on every side no bound is seen”)
mean that the true and constant stands alone revealed, belonging to nothing, the whole earth bright and clear without the least obstruction. The third line
(“I sit in stillness, unknown to all”)

means that the wondrous substance of suchness—worldlings certainly cannot know it, and the Buddhas of the three times cannot find where I am either; hence “unknown to all.” The three lines “a lonely moon on the cold spring”
(“A lonely moon on the cold spring; within the spring there is no moon; the moon is there in the blue sky”—these three lines)
are the old man’s skilful simile for this state. In the last two lines
(“I sing this little song of mine: within the song no Chan you’ll find”)
he fears that people will take the finger for the moon, and so he especially warns us: language and words are not Chan at all!

[Taking the finger for the moon]Mistaking the finger that points at the moon for the moon itself. [Language and words are not Chan]Words that speak of Chan point toward Chan; they are not Chan itself.
Excerpted from the Chronicle of Master Xuyun.

Four of the seven days’ morning light have already gone, and you have all been working hard. Some of you have written poems and verses and come to my place to ask about them—this too is rare. But working as you do, you have forgotten what I said the two days before. Last night I said, ‘In practice there is no other practice; one need only know the road’s head’
(‘In practice there is no other practice; one need only know the road’s head. If the road’s head is known, birth-and-death both come to rest.’)
. We are now investigating the huatou, and the huatou
(the head of the word)

is precisely the road’s head we should walk. Our aim is to attain Buddhahood and end birth-and-death; to end birth-and-death, we must borrow this huatou as a vajra-king sword: when a demon comes, cut down the demon; when a Buddha comes, cut down the Buddha; leave not one feeling, establish not one dharma. Where, then, is there room for so many idle thoughts—writing poems and verses, seeing emptiness and seeing light, and the like? If you work in this way, I do not know where your huatou has gone. I say no more to the old practitioners; but those who have newly aroused the mind must take care!

Because I feared that you would not know how to work, I spent the past two days explaining one by one the causes and conditions of this retreat, the value of this method in our school, and the way to work at it. Our way of working is simply to raise a single huatou, day and night at all six periods, like flowing water, never letting it break off. Keep it bright and undimmed, clearly and constantly known, and cut all ordinary feelings and noble understandings clean away at a single stroke. The ancients said, ‘Learning the Way is like guarding a fortress city; grip the wall and fight a battle. If you have not endured a bone-piercing cold, how shall the plum blossom’s fragrance reach your nose?’ This was said by Chan Master Huangbo. These four lines carry two meanings. The first two are a simile: we who work at practice guard this huatou as one guards a fortress city, letting no one in or out—a guarding of the strictest kind. For each of us has a mind-king, and this mind-king is the eighth consciousness. Outside the eighth consciousness there are also the seventh consciousness
(manas)
, the sixth consciousness
(mental consciousness)
, and the first five consciousnesses
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness)

, and so on. Those first five are the five thieves of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the sixth consciousness is the thief of mind; the seventh is manas. It—manas—from morning to night greedily clings to the seeing aspect of the eighth consciousness as a self, rouses the sixth consciousness, and leads the first five consciousnesses to crave the dust-realms of form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, so that delusion and affliction never cease, and the mind-king of the eight consciousnesses

(The mind-king is the mental subject capable of taking external objects as its conditions, the root of cognition; this mind-king contains eight consciousnesses—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, manas, and ālaya—and so is also called the “mind-king of the eight consciousnesses.”)

is bound so tightly that it cannot turn itself around. So today we must borrow this huatou (the vajra-king sword) to kill those robbers, so that the eighth consciousness turns into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the seventh into the Wisdom of Equality, the sixth into the Wisdom of Wonderful Observation, and the first five into the Wisdom of Perfectly Accomplished Action. But the most important thing is to turn the sixth and seventh consciousnesses first, for they have a leading role, and their power is precisely their ability to discriminate and calculate. Now, when you write poems and verses, see emptiness and see light, it is these two consciousnesses at work. Today we must borrow this huatou to turn the discriminating consciousness into the Wisdom of Wonderful Observation and the mind that calculates self and other into the Wisdom of Equality—this is called turning consciousness into wisdom, turning the ordinary into the noble. We must make it so that the thieves who have always craved form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas cannot trespass; hence the words ‘like guarding a fortress city.’

[Turning consciousness into wisdom]Turning the ordinary being’s defiled eight consciousnesses into the Buddha’s four wisdoms: the eighth consciousness (ālaya) into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the seventh (manas) into the Wisdom of Equality, the sixth (mental consciousness) into the Wisdom of Wonderful Observation, and the first five (eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness) into the Wisdom of Perfectly Accomplished Action.
(See in detail
Turning Consciousness into Wisdom
)[Defiled]

Defilement (āsrava) is another name for affliction; “defiled” means having affliction. Āsrava carries two senses, outflow and falling: afflictions such as greed and hatred flow out and stream down day and night through the six sense-gates without ceasing—this is called āsrava; and again, afflictions cause one to fall into the three evil paths—this too is called āsrava. Therefore every dharma that has affliction is called a defiled dharma, and all conditioned dharmas in the world are defiled dharmas that have affliction.

The last two lines, the simile ‘If you have not endured a bone-piercing cold, how shall the plum blossom’s fragrance reach your nose?’, mean this: we beings of the three realms are sunk in the sea of birth-and-death, entangled by the five desires, deluded by the toils of dust, and unable to win liberation. So the plum blossom is taken as a simile, because the plum blossom opens in snowy weather. All things in the world are born in spring, grow in summer, harvested in autumn, and stored in winter. In winter the weather is cold, and insects and plants alike are frozen to death or withdrawn into store; even the dust lies quiet and cool within the snow and cannot rise. These insects, plants, and dusty, turbid things are like the idle thoughts, discrimination, ignorance, jealousy, and the rest of the three-poison afflictions in our minds. When we do away with these things, the mind-king is naturally at ease—just as the plum blossom opens and gives forth fragrance in the snow.

But you should know that this plum blossom can open in ice and snow; it does not appear in bright spring weather or in soft, gentle breezes. If you and I would have the flower of the mind open, it too cannot appear amid joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, or amid the rights and wrongs of self and other. For these eight kinds of mind of ours—if they once turn muddled, they become the neutral nature; if they once do evil, they become the evil nature; if they once do good, they become the good nature. Neutrality includes the neutrality of dreams and the neutrality of vacant nothingness. The neutrality of dreams is the state of being confused in sleep, with only a single dream-scene before one and no knowledge at all of what one did in the day—this is the state of the solitary consciousness, that is, solitary neutrality. As for vacant neutrality, it is like our sitting in meditation now and letting the huatou be lost in the stillness: empty and hollow, muddled and dim, with nothing at all, merely craving a state of quiet. This is the Chan sickness most to be avoided in our practice; this is vacant neutrality. We need only, throughout the twelve periods of day and night, keep a single huatou bright and undimmed, clearly and constantly known—walking thus, sitting thus. Hence the ancients said, ‘Walking, Chan; sitting, Chan; speaking or silent, moving or still, the substance is at peace.’ Master Hanshan said: ‘High atop the mountain peak, on every side no bound is seen; I sit in stillness, unknown to all, a lonely moon on the cold spring. Within the spring there is no moon; the moon is there in the blue sky. I sing this little song of mine: within the song no Chan you’ll find.’ You and I are all joined by karmic affinity, and so I have spoken these words on practice to you once more. I hope you will strive and advance diligently, and not use your minds on sundry matters.

Let me tell one more koan. Long ago the founding patriarch of Xitan Monastery on Mount Jizu, after leaving home, travelled to pay respects and study in many places, working at the Way with great diligence. One day, lodging at an inn, he heard the daughter of a bean-curd shop next door singing: ‘Zhang’s bean curd, Li’s bean curd; a thousand roads pondered on the pillow—tomorrow it is bean curd again.’ At that moment this patriarch was sitting in meditation; hearing her song, he awakened at once. From this we can see that the ancients’ effort did not have to be made in a Chan hall for one to work or to awaken to the Way. In practice, the precious thing is single-mindedness. None of you should let your mind wander and scatter and pass the time in vain; otherwise, tomorrow you will still be selling bean curd.

In the matter of practice: where it is easy, it is truly easy; where it is hard, it is truly hard. Easy, because if only you can let go, believe firmly, and arouse a steadfast mind and a long-enduring mind, you may succeed. Hard, because you and I fear hardship and seek comfort and pleasure, not knowing that even all the conditioned dharmas in the world require a course of learning before they can be mastered—how much more so when we would learn to be sages and worthies, would attain Buddhahood and become patriarchs? How could that be done in a slapdash way?

Therefore, first you must have a steadfast mind. For one who practices the Way can never escape demonic obstacles; demonic obstacles are the toils of dust and karmic states of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas that I spoke of yesterday. These karmic states are your and my sworn enemies in birth-and-death, which is why many Dharma masters who expound sutras also cannot keep their footing in such states—the cause is a mind of the Way that is not steadfast.

Next, you must arouse a long-enduring mind. We live in this world creating boundless karma; once we would practice and seek to end birth-and-death and escape death, how could we put down our habitual tendencies all at once? The patriarchs of old: Chan Master Changqing sat until he wore through seven sitting cushions; Zhaozhou was eighty years old and still wandering on pilgrimage, watching the single word ‘wu’ for forty years without letting his mind stray. Later he was greatly awakened; the King of Yan and the King of Zhao revered him deeply and made all kinds of offerings to him; and in the Qing dynasty the Yongzheng Emperor, reading his recorded sayings and finding them lofty, bestowed on him the title Ancient Buddha. All of these succeeded through a lifetime of ascetic practice. If you and I would put down our habitual tendencies and faults altogether and clarify a single thought, we would be the equal of the Buddhas and patriarchs. As the Shurangama Sutra says: ‘It is like clarifying muddy water stored in a clean vessel: when it is still and deeply unmoving, the sand and earth settle of themselves, and the clear water appears—this is called the initial subduing of the affliction of guest-dust. When the mud is gone and only pure water remains, it is called the eternal severing of fundamental ignorance.’ Your and my habitual tendencies and afflictions are like mud and silt; hence we must use the huatou. The huatou is like clear alum, which can make muddy water settle and clear (that is, subdue the afflictions).

If a practitioner reaches the point where body and mind are one and a still state appears before him, he must take care not to shuffle forward like a woman with bound feet. He should know that this is only the first stage of effort; the silt of affliction and ignorance is not yet cut off. This is to go from an afflicted mind to clarity, like muddy water settling into clear water. Even so, the silt at the bottom is not yet gone, and so he must add effort and press on. The ancients said, ‘One who sits atop the hundred-foot pole, though he has seen, has not yet the truth; if he can step forward again from the pole, the ten directions appear as the whole body.’ If he does not press on, then he takes the conjured city for his home, and afflictions still have occasion to arise. In that case even to be a self-liberated one is very difficult; hence one must remove the mud and keep the water, and only then is fundamental ignorance eternally cut off—only then is Buddhahood attained.

When ignorance is eternally cut off, you may appear anywhere in the ten directions to teach the Dharma: like Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva’s thirty-two manifestations—whatever body one should be saved by, he manifests that body and speaks the Dharma for them. Whether in houses of lust or wine shops, in the wombs of oxen, horses, or mules, in heaven or in hell, you are utterly free and unfettered. Otherwise, a single errant thought and you are in the six paths of rebirth. Long ago Qin Hui served as incense-and-lamp attendant before Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, but because he did not arouse a long-enduring mind and did not cut off the affliction of ignorance, he was undone by his own anger—this is one example. If your faith is firm and your long-enduring mind does not retreat, then no matter how ordinary a person you are, you may attain Buddhahood in this very body.

The ancients said, ‘The sun and moon fly like a shuttle; time is like an arrow.’ It seems but yesterday that the retreat began, and tomorrow is already the day of release. By the rules, tomorrow morning there will be an examination of your effort. For the retreat is a means of realizing the fruit within a set term: to realize is to awaken, to see one’s own original scenery, to awaken to the Tathāgata’s wondrous nature—hence “realizing-awakening.” The examination is to look into what degree your effort has reached in these seven days and to have you reveal it before the assembly. Ordinarily, to examine you at this time is called collecting the bun money; everyone must pay it. It means that everyone in this retreat should awaken, and everyone may spread the Buddhadharma and save all beings. Now, not to speak of everyone awakening—if even one person awakens, he can pay back the bun money: as the saying goes, the crowd eats and one person settles the bill. If we arouse a single mind of diligent effort, it is possible for everyone to awaken.

The ancients said, ‘For a worldling to become a Buddha is truly easy; to remove idle thoughts is truly hard.’ It is only because you and I, since beginningless time, have burned with craving and love, wandered in birth-and-death, and with eighty-four thousand toils of dust and every kind of habitual fault cannot let go, that we do not awaken to the Way, unlike the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who are ever awake and never deluded. Therefore Lianchi said: ‘Defiling conditions are easy to meet; the work of the Way is hard to accomplish. Not understanding the differences among the ten thousand conditions before one, one sees only the wind of conditions raging, withering the forest of merit, and the fire of the mind blazing, burning up the seeds of bodhi. If the thought of the Way were like the thought of love, one would long since have become a Buddha. Do for others as for yourself, and both matters are settled; do not see others’ faults or your own merits, and naturally you will be reverent above and respectful below; the Buddhadharma will appear at every moment, and affliction will be loosed in every dust-mote.’ These dozen or so lines—how clear and how true they are!

‘Defiling’ means staining. The state of a worldling is always to crave and be stained by wealth, beauty, fame, and profit, and to be angry and contentious. To the two words ‘morality and virtue’ they treat them as stumbling stones. From morning to night they pass through joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, craving wealth, honour, and splendour; one worldly feeling after another never ends, and not a trace of the thought of the Way remains. So the forest of merit is withered and the seeds of bodhi burned up. If one looked upon worldly feelings lightly, regarded all kin and all foes as equal, did not kill, did not steal, did not commit sexual misconduct, did not speak falsely, did not drink wine, saw all beings as equal and without distinction, saw others’ hunger as one’s own hunger and others’ drowning as one’s own drowning, and constantly aroused the bodhi mind, then one would accord with the thought of the Way and could become a Buddha on the spot. Hence the words: ‘If the thought of the Way were like the thought of love, one would long since have become a Buddha.’ The Buddhas, sages, and worthies who respond and manifest in the world do everything in service of beings—what is called pulling out suffering and giving happiness, rousing compassion and aiding beings. If you and I can master ourselves and return to propriety, and use nothing for our own enjoyment, then everyone will be free of hardship and everything can be accomplished, and at the same time you yourself will receive the reward of perfect fruition. As when the water in river and stream rises, the boat rises of itself.

If you can treat others with a compassionate mind and a respectful mind, neither exalting yourself nor belittling yourself, neither proud nor false, then those who see you will surely be respectful and courteous. Otherwise, relying only on your own abilities, putting on the airs of an elder, or saying one thing and meaning another, scheming only for pleasure and for fame—then even if people are respectful to you, I fear it is false. Hence Confucius said, ‘He who respects others is constantly respected by them; he who loves others is constantly loved by them.’ The Sixth Patriarch said, ‘Let others be wrong; I am not wrong. If I am wrong, then I have a fault.’ Therefore we must never give rise to a mind that makes right and wrong, or draws lines between self and other. If we serve others as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do, then bodhi seeds will be sown everywhere, and the fruits of goodness harvested at every moment; affliction will naturally find no hold on you. The three baskets and twelve divisions of sutras spoken by the World-Honoured One were likewise for the sake of our three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion. Hence the heart of the three baskets and twelve divisions is precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and cause and effect: to make us renounce craving, hold fast to compassion, joy, and equanimity, practise the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, break through delusion, error, and folly, perfect the marks of wisdom and virtue, and adorn the dharmakāya of merit. If one can conduct oneself in the world in this way, then truly every place is the Huazang realm.

Now, to speak from the standpoint of study and practice, we should always hold rules and methods in honour. The resident community has aroused the mind of the Way, expounding sutras and holding retreats and spreading the Buddhadharma—truly a rare and hard-won karmic condition. You have all braved wind and dust and feared no weariness; busy as you are, you have come willingly to take part, and clearly you all have a mind weary of turmoil and longing for stillness. Originally you and I are of one mind; the difference lies only in delusion and awakening. Hence there are beings who toil all day with never a day’s leisure—if one thinks about it a little, it is truly without benefit. But there is a kind of person who, all his life, rushes about day and night, foolishly dreaming of ample clothing and food, coveting song-stages and dance pavilions, wishing only that sons and grandsons be rich and noble with glory for ten thousand generations. When his last breath fails and he has become a ghost, he still wants to bless his children with prosperity in people and wealth—such a person is utterly foolish. There is another kind who knows a little about good and evil, cause and effect, and wishes to do meritorious deeds, but knows only to give vegetarian feasts and make offerings to monks, or to cast Buddha images, or to repair temples—all defiled causes—hoping for blessings in the next life. Because he does not understand the preciousness of undefiled merit, he rejects it and does not practise it.

The Lotus Sutra says, ‘If a person sits in stillness for a single instant, that surpasses the building of seven-jewel stupas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.’ For the practice of sitting in stillness can free us from the toils of dust, bring peace to body and mind, make our own nature perfect and bright, and end birth-and-death. A single instant means the space of one moment, one snap of the fingers. If a person with a pure, still mind turns the light around and reflects inward, and sits for the length of a single instant, even if he cannot awaken to the Way, the Buddha-nature as primary cause has already been planted in him, and the day of his accomplishment will come. If his effort has power, then within a single instant he can become a Buddha. Hence in the Shurangama Sutra the Venerable Ānanda says, ‘Without passing through asamkhyeya kalpas, I obtain the dharmakāya.’ But you and I and ordinary people live always amid the toils of dust, amid joy and anger, amid gain and loss, amid the five desires, amid every pursuit of pleasure and enjoyment. Now when you enter the Chan hall and the signal for stillness sounds, you see nothing and hear nothing; the six sense-gates are like the turtle withdrawing its six limbs, and no state whatsoever can disturb you. This is practising the unconditioned Dharma, the undefiled Dharma. Hence stupas built of the seven treasures, gold and silver and the rest, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, still cannot equal the merit of this single instant of sitting in stillness. The turtle withdrawing its six limbs is a simile: the sea-dog delights in eating fish and turtles, and when it sees a turtle crawling on the beach it runs to eat it. The turtle, knowing it means to eat it, draws its four legs, its head, and its tail all into its shell; the sea-dog sees it and cannot bite it, wastes its effort, and goes away, and at that moment the turtle escapes the danger. We who live in this world—the poor busy unto death for clothing and food, the rich craving form and desire and unable to escape—are just like being bitten by the sea-dog. If one knows the harm, one draws in the six sense-gates
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind)
and turns the light around and reflects inward, and can come back to life from death.

The ancients said, ‘A hundred years, thirty-six thousand days—not one moment given to stilling body and mind.’ You and I who have wandered in birth-and-death through measureless kalpas do so only because we will not let go of body and mind and practise in purity, and so we receive rebirth and cannot be freed. Therefore everyone should let go of body and mind and come to sit in stillness for a while, hoping that the lacquer bucket will drop away and that we may together realize the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas.

blocks.text: Seeing the Nature Through and Through

inline.s: According to
the Autobiographical Chronicle of Master Xuyun, it is recorded:

In the twenty-first year of the Guangxu reign, the year yiwei (1895), Elder Master Xuyun was fifty-six. That year, Gaomin Monastery in Yangzhou planned to hold twelve consecutive Chan retreats. Elder Master Xuyun, urged on by the assembly, went to Gaomin for the retreats. After descending the mountain to Digang in Datong and walking along the river, he suddenly met a great flood and could not go on. He meant to cross by boat, but having not a penny on him, the boatman actually pulled up his oars and left. Left with no choice, Elder Master Xuyun had to struggle on along the river. Then he lost his footing and fell into the water, drifting up and down with the current for a whole day and night. He floated to somewhere near Caishi Rock, where fortunately fishermen rescued him and carried him to nearby Baoji Monastery. When he came to, blood would not stop flowing from his mouth, his nose, and the openings of his bowels and bladder. After resting quietly for several days, afraid of missing the retreat, he forced himself up and went straight to Gaomin Monastery.

At Gaomin Monastery, Elder Master Xuyun said nothing at all about his falling into the water or his illness. The monk in charge told him to serve in the Chan hall in another’s place, but Elder Master Xuyun, his strength failing, did not accept. Gaomin Monastery was long known for the severity of its house style: whoever was asked to serve and refused was regarded as slighting the assembly

and so Elder Master Xuyun received a beating with the incense board. After the beating his illness grew worse, the bleeding would not stop, and he passed semen in his urine. Yet he accepted it all in silence, offering not a single word of explanation. In the Chan hall he held out against death, keeping to his sitting, day and night diligent, clarifying a single thought, until he no longer knew what his body was. After more than twenty days of fierce effort,
all his illnesses were suddenly
healed.

Later, Chan Master De’an, abbot of Baoji Monastery at Caishi Rock, sent clothing to Gaomin Monastery as an offering to the community, and seeing Elder Master Xuyun’s radiant face, was greatly astonished and delighted. He then told the community at Gaomin how Elder Master Xuyun had fallen into the water. When the community heard it, all were filled with admiration
and the Chan hall
also
no longer arranged for him to take his turn at duties. Elder Master Xuyun thus gained the freedom to practise single-mindedly,
from then on
and ten thousand thoughts suddenly ceased
his effort settled home,
and day and night were as one, his movements like flying.

[Settled home]“Settled home” means “made solid.” Elder Master Xuyun said: ‘Only in Buddha-recitation must one gather the mind and contemplate, so that every phrase settles home. Settling home means making solid. When every phrase is solid and every thought corresponds, in time they become one piece. From the one mind of practice one arrives at the one mind of principle; subject and object are both forgotten, self and other are not two—how is this different from investigating Chan?’ (Casual Instructions of Elder Master Xuyun)

One evening, at the time of the evening incense, Elder Master Xuyun suddenly opened his eyes and saw before him a single expanse of light, bright as day, within and without perfectly clear. Through the wall he saw the incense-and-lamp attendant urinating, and he saw Master Xidan defecating in the latrine. Looking further into the distance, he saw boats moving on the river and the trees on both banks—every shape and colour, each one seen distinctly. The next day Elder Master Xuyun asked the incense-and-lamp attendant and Master Xidan about the matter, and it was indeed so. Yet Elder Master Xuyun did not take it to heart, regarding it merely as an ordinary state.

On the third night of the eighth Chan retreat in the twelfth month, when the sixth incense ended and stillness was released, the retreat-attendant Dharma master routinely poured hot water for each of the meditating masters. When the attendant poured hot water for Elder Master Xuyun, he was careless, and the hot water splashed onto Elder Master Xuyun’s hand; the teacup fell to the ground and shattered. At that very moment Elder Master Xuyun cut through the root of doubt and was filled with joy for the first time in his life, as if waking from a dream. He thought to himself: having left home and wandered for decades, had he not fallen into the water and fallen gravely ill this time, had he not met with both the gentle and the harsh
means, and the
teaching of a good and wise teacher, he would almost have missed this whole life—how could there be today’s awakening to the Way! Thereupon he composed a verse:
The cup went crashing to the ground; / the sound rang out, clear and distinct.
The void itself is shattered through; / the mad mind ceases in that instant.
There was another verse:
A scalded hand, a broken cup; / a ruined home, dear ones gone—no words come up.
When spring arrives, the flowers bloom and all is fair; / the hills, the rivers, the great earth—the Tathāgata is there.
Dharma Master Shaoyun, in
Master Xuyun at Mount Yunju
, records

When the old Master rested at noon, he would sometimes doze, his head nodding forward, and even snore. Once, hearing him snore, we slipped away quietly, took the fruit from the room, and went outside to eat and play. When he woke, he scolded us for each thing we had done. We asked:
Just now, were you not asleep and snoring, old Master? How did you know?
He said:
I know even how many idle thoughts pass through your mind; you took things outside to eat—would I not know?

From then on we believed that one who has awakened to the Way and ended birth-and-death has already broken through the five aggregates. He looked asleep, yet his mind was perfectly clear and distinct.
We also took the opportunity to ask the old Master about his days living in a thatched hut at Zhongnan Mountain.

That year the old Master was sixty-seven and living in a thatched hut at Zhongnan Mountain. Dharma Master Jiechen, a master who lectured on the great sutras, heard that the old Master had awakened at Gaomin Monastery, and came to the thatched hut at Zhongnan Mountain to debate the pivotal sayings of Chan with him. Hearing him speak in such grand terms, the old Master said to him:

Your pivotal debate is excellent, but it is not your own true effort; on the fundamental matter of birth-and-death you cannot be your own master, and King Yama will not let you off. Debate no more—let the two of us sit and see.

So the two of them sat in meditation in the thatched hut. The old Master sat for seven days and seven nights without moving. But Dharma Master Jiechen sat only half a day before his legs ached unbearably, and the idle thoughts in his mind grew more and more restless.
